goldens.comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
goldens.reasoning: C1 points out the same problem: canManage() falls back to the VIEW scope as well as MANAGE, which gives write access to principals that should only be able to view.

goldens.comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
goldens.reasoning: C2 points out the same mismatch: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses the authz resource id (groupResource.getId()) where the group id or resource name is expected. This breaks group filtering in UserModel.GROUPS.

candidates: canManage() falls back to hasPermission(... VIEW, MANAGE), which means a principal with only view on Groups could satisfy auth.groups().requireManage() (e.g., GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup). That seems to broaden write access beyond manage scope and could allow unintended group modifications.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() uses groupResource.getId() (authz resource id) as if it were the Keycloak group id; hasPermission() also expects an identifier that can be resolved via resourceStore.findByName() (i.e., the resource name). This likely breaks group-scoped user visibility and can populate UserModel.GROUPS with unusable identifiers.

In hasPermission, when no group-specific resource exists you call getResourceTypeResource(...) and then immediately policyStore.findByResource(server, resource); if resource is null (schema not initialized / missing resource), this will NPE. Consider handling a missing resource-type resource by returning false.
